questions.text:
Expedite, Hasten, Hurry, __________

Fill the blank by choosing a word with a meaning similar to that of the words given above.
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: Expedite, hasten and hurry all mean to make something happen faster. Accelerate has the same meaning. Retard means to slow down, while provide and disable are unrelated.

questions.text: A black square PQRS has been cut into two parts. One part of it is shown in Panel I. Which one of the shapes in Panel II is the other part?
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution:
Treat the square as a 6 by 6 grid. Reading the empty cells of Panel I row by row (inside the border, columns 2 to 6):

Row 2: columns 2, 5, 6

Row 3: columns 2, 3, 4, 5

Row 4: column 4

Row 5: columns 2, 3, 4

So the missing piece has a top row with one cell, a gap of two and then two cells; a full row of four below it; a single stem cell under the third column; and a bottom bar of three cells starting from the left. Shape (iii) is exactly this, in the same orientation. Shape (i) has a bottom bar of four cells, (ii) has its bottom bar shifted right, and (iv) has a wider stem.

questions.text: A day can only be cloudy or sunny. The probability of a day being cloudy is 0.5, independent of the condition on other days. What is the probability that in any given four days, there will be three cloudy days and one sunny day?
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution:
The sunny day can be any one of the four days, so there are \(\binom{4}{3} = 4\) favourable patterns, each with probability \((0.5)^4 = \frac{1}{16}\).

\[P = 4 \times \frac{1}{16} = \frac{1}{4}\]

questions.text: The values of Stock A and Stock B on a particular day are Rs. 50 and Rs. 80, respectively. An investor invests Rs. 100 in Stock A and Rs. 80 in Stock B. He sells all the stocks the next day when the value of Stock A is Rs. 55 and Stock B is Rs. 70. The profit made by the investor is Rs. ________
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution:
Rs. 100 buys \(100/50 = 2\) shares of A, and Rs. 80 buys \(80/80 = 1\) share of B. Total invested: Rs. 180.

Next day: \(2 \times 55 + 1 \times 70 = 110 + 70 = 180\).

Profit \(= 180 - 180 = 0\).

questions.text:
‘When it is raining, peacocks dance.’

Based only on this sentence, which one of the following options is necessarily true?

options.label: A
options.text: Peacocks dance only when it is raining.

options.label: B
options.text: When peacocks dance, it is raining.

options.label: C
options.text: When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.

options.label: D
options.text: When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance.

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution:
The sentence says: raining \(\rightarrow\) peacocks dance. The only statement that must follow is its contrapositive: peacocks not dancing \(\rightarrow\) not raining, which is option C.

Options A and B are the converse, and D is the inverse. Neither follows, since peacocks may dance when it is not raining.

questions.text:
Water : P :: Food : Q

Choose the P and Q combination from the options below to form a meaningful analogy.
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: Water satisfies thirst, and food satisfies hunger. So P = Thirst and Q = Hunger. In B the two relations differ (drink is an action, hunger a need), and C and D break the parallel.

questions.text: Two tiles are missing in Panel I. Which one of the options in Panel II is the appropriate choice for the missing tiles?
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution:
Count the black dots in each tile of Panel I:

| 8 | 1 | 6 |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 5 | ? |
| 4 | 9 | ? |

The first row adds to 15 and the first two columns add to 15 (\(8 + 3 + 4\) and \(1 + 5 + 9\)). This is the 3 by 3 magic square, so the missing tiles hold \(15 - 3 - 5 = 7\) and \(15 - 4 - 9 = 2\) black dots (and \(6 + 7 + 2 = 15\) for the last column).

The dots also fill in a fixed order: right column from the bottom up, then the middle column from the bottom up, then the left column from the bottom up. With 7 dots the right and middle columns are full and only the bottom left dot is black; with 2 dots the lower two dots of the right column are black. Option (i) shows exactly this. (ii) has 6 and 2, (iii) has 7 and 3, and (iv) has 6 and 4.

questions.text:
Figures (i) and (ii) represent intercity highway systems. The black dots represent cities and the line segments between them represent intercity highways.

A salesperson needs to make a trip. She needs to start from a city, visit each of the remaining cities exactly once, and finally return to the same city from which she started.

Which one of the following options is then true?

options.label: A
options.text: Such a trip is possible for (i), but not for (ii).

options.label: B
options.text: Such a trip is possible for (ii), but not for (i).

options.label: C
options.text: Such a trip is possible for both (i) and (ii).

options.label: D
options.text: Such a trip is possible neither for (i) nor for (ii).

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution:
The trip is a cycle through every city exactly once.

(i) is a 4 by 4 grid of 16 cities. Go along the top row, then snake down and back through the lower rows using columns 2 to 4, and return up the first column: such a closed tour visiting all 16 cities exists, so the trip is possible.

(ii) has 5 cities. Call the top left city A and the bottom city E. The other three cities (top right, inner, left) each have exactly two highways, both going to A and E. A closed tour must use both highways of every degree 2 city, so A would need three highways in the tour, but a city on a cycle uses exactly two. So the trip is impossible for (ii).

questions.text: The figure in Panel I below is a grid of cells with four rows and four columns. The numbers on the top and on the left represent the number of cells that are to be shaded in that column and row, respectively. Which one of the options shown in Panel II below represents the grid shaded correctly?
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution:
Required: rows 3, 1, 2, 2 and every column 2.

(i): row 2 has 2 shaded cells, not 1. Wrong.

(ii): rows have 3, 1, 2, 2 shaded cells. Columns: column 1 (rows 1, 4), column 2 (rows 2, 4), column 3 (rows 1, 3), column 4 (rows 1, 3), each 2. Correct.

(iii): row 2 has 2 shaded cells. Wrong.

(iv): row 4 has 3 shaded cells. Wrong.

questions.text: An unbiased six-faced dice whose faces are marked with numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 is rolled twice in succession and the number on the top face is recorded each time. The probability that the sum of the two recorded numbers is a prime number is ________
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution:
Possible prime sums are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11. Number of ordered outcomes: sum 2: 1, sum 3: 2, sum 5: 4, sum 7: 6, sum 11: 2. Total = 15.

\[P = \frac{15}{36}\]

questions.text:
For two different persons \(x\) and \(y\), the predicate \(M(x, y)\) denotes that x knows y.

Consider the following statement.

There is a person who does not know anyone else, but that person is known by everyone else.

Which one of the following expressions represents the above statement?

options.label: A
options.text: \((\exists y)(\forall x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow (M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))\)

options.label: B
options.text: \((\forall y)(\exists x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow (M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))\)

options.label: C
options.text: \((\exists y)(\exists x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow (M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))\)

options.label: D
options.text: \((\forall y)(\forall x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow (M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))\)

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let \(y\) be the special person. We need: there exists \(y\) such that for every other person \(x\), \(x\) knows \(y\) (\(M(x, y)\)) and \(y\) does not know \(x\) (\(\neg M(y, x)\)). That is

\[(\exists y)(\forall x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow (M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))\]

which is option A. B says everyone has such a relation with someone, C needs only one other person, and D says it holds for every pair, all different statements.

questions.text:
The set T represents various traversals over binary tree. The set S represents the order of visiting nodes during a traversal.

| T | S |
|---|---|
| I: Inorder | L: left subtree, node, right subtree |
| II: Preorder | M: node, left subtree, right subtree |
| III: Postorder | N: left subtree, right subtree, node |

Which one of the following is the correct match from T to S ?

options.label: A
options.text: I – L, II – M, III – N

options.label: B
options.text: I – M, II – L, III – N

options.label: C
options.text: I – N, II – M, III – L

options.label: D
options.text: I – L, II – N, III – M

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.chapter: Trees, Binary Search Trees and Heaps
questions.solution: Inorder visits left subtree, node, right subtree (L). Preorder visits the node first, then left and right (M). Postorder visits left, right, then the node (N). So I with L, II with M, III with N.

questions.text:
Which one of the following statements is equivalent to the following assertion?

Turing machine \(M\) decides the language \(L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*\)

options.label: A
options.text: Turing machine \(M\) halts on all input strings in \(\{0,1\}^*\)

options.label: B
options.text: Turing machine \(M\) accepts all input strings in \(L\)

options.label: C
options.text: Turing machine \(M\) rejects all input strings in \(\{0,1\}^* - L\)

options.label: D
options.text: Turing machine \(M\) accepts all input strings in \(L\) and rejects all input strings in \(\{0,1\}^* - L\)

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.solution:
\(M\) decides \(L\) when it halts on every input, accepting exactly the strings of \(L\) and rejecting every string outside \(L\). Option D states exactly this (accepting and rejecting both mean halting).

A alone says nothing about which strings are accepted. B alone allows \(M\) to loop on strings outside \(L\) (that only recognises \(L\)). C alone allows \(M\) to loop or reject on strings of \(L\).

questions.text:
The probability density function \(f(x)\) of a random variable \(X\) which takes real values is

\[f(x) = \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{18}\right), \quad x \in (-\infty, +\infty)\]

Which one of the following statements is correct about the random variable \(X\) ?
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
The normal density is \(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\). With \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma = 3\), \(2\sigma^2 = 18\), which is exactly the given \(f(x)\). So \(X\) is normal with mean 0 and variance 9.

An exponential density is zero for negative \(x\), a Poisson variable is discrete, and a uniform density is constant on an interval.

questions.text:
In the context of DBMS, consider the two sets T and S given below.

| T | S |
|---|---|
| I: Logical schema | L: Views |
| II: Physical schema | M: File organization and indexes |
| III: External schema | N: Relations |

Which one of the following is the correct match from T to S ?

options.label: A
options.text: I – L, II – M, III – N

options.label: B
options.text: I – M, II – L, III – N

options.label: C
options.text: I – N, II – M, III – L

options.label: D
options.text: I – N, II – L, III – M

questions.subject: Databases
questions.solution: The logical (conceptual) schema describes the relations stored in the database (N). The physical schema describes how the data is stored: file organization and indexes (M). The external schema is what users see, defined through views (L). So I with N, II with M, III with L.

questions.text:
Which one of the following options is not a property of Boolean Algebra?

Note: + is OR operation, . is AND operation, and ′ is NOT operation
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution: A and D are the commutative laws, and C is the complement law for OR. For AND the complement law is \(a \cdot a' = 0\), not 1 (if \(a = 1\) then \(a' = 0\) and the product is 0). So B is not a property.

questions.text: In C runtime environment, which one of the following is stored in heap?

options.label: A
options.text: A static variable declared inside a function

options.label: B
options.text: An array of integers declared inside a function

options.label: C
options.text: A dynamically allocated array of integers created using malloc() function call

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.solution: Memory returned by malloc() comes from the heap. A static local variable lives in the static data segment, an ordinary local array lives in the function's stack frame, and the return address is saved on the stack.

questions.text:
Consider the following two statements about interrupt handling mechanisms in a CPU.

S1: In non-vectored interrupt mechanism, it usually takes more time to start the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) when compared to that in a vectored interrupt mechanism.

S2: In daisy-chain interrupt mechanism, the CPU polls all the input devices individually to determine the source of the interrupt.

Which one of the following options is correct with respect to S1 and S2 ?

options.label: A
options.text: Both S1 and S2 are true

options.label: B
options.text: Both S1 and S2 are false

options.label: C
options.text: S1 is true and S2 is false

options.label: D
options.text: S1 is false and S2 is true

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.solution:
S1: with vectored interrupts the device supplies the ISR address directly. With non-vectored interrupts the CPU jumps to a common routine that must then find the source, so starting the right ISR takes longer. True.

S2: in a daisy chain the interrupt acknowledge signal passes from device to device in hardware, and the first requesting device puts its identity on the bus. The CPU does not poll each device in software (that is the polling method). False.

options.label: A
options.text: Only P1 will compile without any error

options.label: B
options.text: Only P2 will compile without any error

options.label: C
options.text: Only P3 will compile without any error

options.label: D
options.text: All three programs P1, P2, and P3 will compile without any error

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
P1: the local a inside main is in a different scope from the global a, so it simply shadows it. Compiles.

P2: a is declared twice in the same block scope. Redeclaration error.

P3: a is declared twice in the same block with different types. Error (conflicting types).

So only P1 compiles.

questions.text: Consider concurrent execution of two transactions \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) in a DBMS, both of which access a data object \(A\). For these two transactions to not conflict on \(A\), which one of the following statements must be true?
questions.subject: Databases
questions.solution: Two operations of different transactions on the same item conflict when at least one of them is a write. Read and write, write and read, and write and write all conflict. Only when both transactions just read \(A\) is there no conflict.

questions.text:
Consider a file of size 4 million bytes being transferred between two hosts connected via a path consisting of three consecutive links of bandwidth 2 Mbps, 500 kbps, and 1 Mbps, respectively. All processing delays and propagation delays are negligible. Assume that there is no other background traffic over the path and no other additional overhead to transfer the file.

Which one of the following is the total time (in seconds) to transfer the file?

Note: \(1\text{M} = 10^6\), \(1\text{k} = 10^3\)
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.solution:
With no overheads and no other traffic, the data streams through the path at the rate of the slowest link, the bottleneck: 500 kbps.

File size \(= 4 \times 10^6 \times 8 = 32 \times 10^6\) bits.

\[t = \frac{32 \times 10^6}{500 \times 10^3} = 64 \text{ s}\]

questions.text: Which one of the following protocols may need to broadcast some of its messages?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.chapter: IP Addressing, Fragmentation and Support Protocols
questions.solution: A new client has no IP address and does not know the DHCP server, so it sends DHCPDISCOVER (and DHCPREQUEST) as broadcasts to 255.255.255.255. SMTP, FTP and HTTP all run over TCP connections to a known server and are unicast.

questions.text: Which one of the following CPU scheduling algorithms cannot be preemptive?
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution: FCFS runs each process until it finishes or blocks, and is non-preemptive by definition. SRTF is the preemptive form of SJF, Round Robin preempts at the end of each time quantum, and priority scheduling can be preemptive.

questions.text:
Consider the following functions, where \(n\) is a positive integer.

\[n^{1/3}, \quad \log(n), \quad \log(n!), \quad 2^{\log(n)}\]

Which one of the following options lists the functions in increasing order of asymptotic growth rate?

Note: Assume the base of log to be 2.
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.solution:
With base 2, \(2^{\log(n)} = n\). By Stirling, \(\log(n!) = \Theta(n \log n)\).

Any positive power of \(n\) beats a logarithm, so \(\log(n) < n^{1/3}\). Then \(n^{1/3} < n < n \log n\).

Order: \(\log(n), n^{1/3}, 2^{\log(n)}, \log(n!)\).

questions.text: Which of the following can be recurrence relation(s) corresponding to an algorithm with time complexity \(\Theta(n)\)?
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.solution:
A: \(T(n) = 1 + 1 + \dots + 1 = n\), so \(\Theta(n)\). Correct.

B: master theorem with \(a = 2\), \(b = 2\), \(f(n) = 1\): \(n^{\log_2 2} = n\) dominates, so \(\Theta(n)\) (exactly \(2n - 1\) for powers of 2). Correct.

C: \(f(n) = n = n^{\log_2 2}\), so \(\Theta(n \log n)\). Wrong.

D: \(T(n) = 1 + 2 + \dots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}\), so \(\Theta(n^2)\). Wrong.

questions.text: Let \(R\) be a binary relation on the set \(\{1, 2, \ldots, 10\}\), where \((x, y) \in R\) if the product of \(x\) and \(y\) is square of an integer. Which of the following properties is/are satisfied by \(R\)?
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
Reflexive: \(x \cdot x = x^2\) is a square for every \(x\). Yes.

Symmetric: \(xy = yx\), so \((x, y) \in R\) gives \((y, x) \in R\). Yes.

Transitive: if \(xy = a^2\) and \(yz = b^2\), then \(xz = \frac{(xy)(yz)}{y^2} = \left(\frac{ab}{y}\right)^2\). This is an integer that is the square of a rational, so it is the square of an integer. Yes. (Equivalently, \(xRy\) exactly when \(x\) and \(y\) have the same square-free part.)

Antisymmetric: \(2 \cdot 8 = 16\), so \((2, 8)\) and \((8, 2)\) are both in \(R\) with \(2 \neq 8\). No.

questions.text: For a real number \(a\), let \(I(a) = \int_{-1}^{1} (3x^2 - ax + 1)\, dx\). Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.label: A
options.text: The value of \(I(a)\) is independent of the value of \(a\)

options.label: B
options.text: The value of \(I(a)\) can vary with the value of \(a\)

options.label: C
options.text: There exists \(a \in (-\infty, +\infty)\) such that \(I(a)\) is a positive real number

options.label: D
options.text: There exists \(a \in (-\infty, +\infty)\) such that \(I(a)\) is a negative real number

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
On the symmetric interval \([-1, 1]\) the odd term \(-ax\) integrates to 0.

\[I(a) = \int_{-1}^{1} 3x^2\, dx + \int_{-1}^{1} 1\, dx = 2 + 2 = 4\]

A: \(I(a) = 4\) for every \(a\). True.

B: it never varies. False.

C: \(I(a) = 4 > 0\) for any \(a\). True.

D: it is never negative. False.

questions.text:
In a system, numbers are represented using 4-bit two’s complement form. Consider four numbers \(N_1 = 1011\), \(N_2 = 1101\), \(N_3 = 1010\) and \(N_4 = 1001\) in the system.

Which of the following operations will result in arithmetic overflow?
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution:
Values: \(N_1 = -5\), \(N_2 = -3\), \(N_3 = -6\), \(N_4 = -7\). The 4-bit range is \(-8\) to \(+7\).

A: \(-5 + (-3) = -8\), representable (1000). No overflow.

B: \(-3 + (-6) = -9\), out of range. Overflow.

C: \(-6 - (-7) = 1\), in range. No overflow.

D: \(-5 + (-7) = -12\), out of range. Overflow.

questions.text: Which of the following grammars is/are ambiguous?
questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.solution:
A: each string \(a^n b^n\) has one derivation (the only choice is how many times to apply \(S \rightarrow aSb\)). Not ambiguous.

B: \(id + id * id\) has two parse trees (+ at the root or * at the root). Ambiguous.

C: the string \(a\) has two parse trees: \(S \rightarrow aS \rightarrow a\) and \(S \rightarrow Sa \rightarrow a\). Ambiguous.

D: right linear, each \(a^n\) has exactly one derivation. Not ambiguous.

questions.text: The keys 5, 28, 19, 15, 26, 33, 12, 17, 10 are inserted into a hash table using the hash function \(h(k) = k \bmod 9\). The collisions are resolved by chaining. After all the keys are inserted, the length of the longest chain is __________. (answer in integer)
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.solution:
\(k \bmod 9\): 5 \(\to\) 5, 28 \(\to\) 1, 19 \(\to\) 1, 15 \(\to\) 6, 26 \(\to\) 8, 33 \(\to\) 6, 12 \(\to\) 3, 17 \(\to\) 8, 10 \(\to\) 1.

Slot 1 gets 28, 19, 10 (3 keys); slots 6 and 8 get 2 each; others at most 1. Longest chain = 3.

questions.text:
Consider the system of linear equations given below.

\[ax + y = b\]
\[16x + ay = 24\]

Suppose the values of a and b are chosen such that the system of linear equations produce multiple solutions. Then the product of a and b is __________. (answer in integer)
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
Multiple solutions need the two equations to be proportional:

\[\frac{a}{16} = \frac{1}{a} = \frac{b}{24}\]

So \(a^2 = 16\), \(a = \pm 4\), and \(b = \frac{24}{a}\).

\(a = 4\): \(b = 6\), \(ab = 24\). \(a = -4\): \(b = -6\), \(ab = 24\).

Either way \(ab = 24\).

questions.text:
Consider an array \(A = [10, 7, 8, 19, 41, 35, 25, 31]\). Suppose the merge sort algorithm is executed on array \(A\) to sort it in increasing order. The merge sort algorithm will carry out a total of 7 merge operations.

A merge operation on sorted left array \(L\) and sorted right array \(R\) is said to be void if the output of the merge operation is the elements of array \(L\) followed by the elements of array \(R\).

The number of void merge operations among these 7 merge operations is __________. (answer in integer)
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.solution:
A merge is void exactly when the last element of \(L\) is at most the first element of \(R\).

Level 1: [10] + [7]: not void. [8] + [19]: void. [41] + [35]: not void. [25] + [31]: void.

Level 2: [7, 10] + [8, 19]: 10 > 8, not void. [35, 41] + [25, 31]: not void.

Level 3: [7, 8, 10, 19] + [25, 31, 35, 41]: 19 < 25, void.

Void merges = 3.

questions.text: If an IP network uses a subnet mask of 255.255.240.0, the maximum number of IP addresses that can be assigned to network interfaces is __________. (answer in integer)
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.chapter: IP Addressing, Fragmentation and Support Protocols
questions.solution:
255.255.240.0 has \(8 + 8 + 4 = 20\) one bits, so 12 host bits and \(2^{12} = 4096\) addresses. The all-zeros (network) and all-ones (broadcast) host addresses cannot be assigned.

\[4096 - 2 = 4094\]

questions.text: The 32-bit IEEE 754 single precision representation of a number is 0xC2710000. The number in decimal representation is ________. (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.subject: Digital Logic

questions.text:
A lexical analyzer uses the following token definitions

- \(letter \rightarrow [A - Za - z]\)
- \(digit \rightarrow [0 - 9]\)
- \(id \rightarrow letter\ (letter \mid digit)^*\)
- \(number \rightarrow digit^+\)
- \(ws \rightarrow (blank \mid tab \mid newline)^+\)

For the string given below,

\[x1 \quad 23mm \quad 78 \quad y \quad 7z \quad zz5 \quad 14A \quad 8H \quad AaYcD\]

the number of tokens (excluding \(ws\)) that will be produced by the lexical analyzer is __________. (answer in integer)
questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.solution:
The analyzer takes the longest match each time. An id must start with a letter, so a digit run ends a number and a following letter starts a new id.

x1: id (1). 23mm: number 23, id mm (2). 78: number (1). y: id (1). 7z: number 7, id z (2). zz5: id (1). 14A: number 14, id A (2). 8H: number 8, id H (2). AaYcD: id (1).

Total \(= 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 13\).

questions.text:
Consider a complete graph \(K_n\) with \(n\) vertices (\(n > 4\)). Note that multiple spanning trees can be constructed over \(K_n\). Each of these spanning trees is represented as a set of edges. The Jaccard coefficient between any two sets is defined as the ratio of the size of the intersection of the two sets to the size of the union of the two sets.

Which one of the following options gives the lowest possible value for the Jaccard coefficient between any two spanning trees of \(K_n\) ?
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
The Jaccard coefficient is 0 when the two trees share no edge, so the question is whether \(K_n\) has two edge-disjoint spanning trees.

\(K_n\) has \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\) edges, at least \(2(n-1)\) when \(n \geq 4\), so there is room for two. A concrete pair on vertices \(1, 2, \ldots, n\):

\(T_1\): the path \(1, 2, 3, \ldots, n\), with edges \(\{i, i+1\}\).

\(T_2\): the edges \(\{1, 3\}, \{1, 4\}, \ldots, \{1, n\}\) together with \(\{2, 4\}\). That is \(n - 1\) edges joining all vertices without a cycle, so it is a spanning tree, and none of its edges joins two consecutive numbers.

The two trees share no edge.

So two spanning trees can have empty intersection, and the lowest possible coefficient is 0.

questions.text: Let \(G\) be a weighted directed acyclic graph with \(m\) edges and \(n\) vertices. Given \(G\) and a source vertex \(s\) in \(G\), which one of the following options gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm to find the lengths of shortest paths from \(s\) to all vertices that are reachable from \(s\) in \(G\)?
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.chapter: Graph Traversals, Spanning Trees and Shortest Paths
questions.solution: In a DAG, topologically sort the vertices in \(\Theta(m + n)\), then relax the outgoing edges of each vertex in that order. Each edge is relaxed once, and every vertex is final when it is processed because all its predecessors come earlier. This works even with negative weights, in \(\Theta(m + n)\) total, and no algorithm can do better since every edge must be read.

questions.text:
Consider an array \(A\) of integers of size \(n\). The indices of \(A\) run from 1 to \(n\). An algorithm is to be designed to check whether \(A\) satisfies the condition given below.

\[\forall i, j \in \{1, \ldots, n-1\} \text{ such that } i > j, \quad (A[i+1] - A[i]) > (A[j+1] - A[j])\]

Which one of the following gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm that can be designed for the problem?
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.solution:
Let \(d_i = A[i+1] - A[i]\). The condition says \(d_i > d_j\) whenever \(i > j\), that is, the sequence \(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_{n-1}\) is strictly increasing. By transitivity it is enough to check \(d_{i+1} > d_i\) for consecutive \(i\): one pass over the array, \(\Theta(n)\).

It cannot be done faster, since changing any single element can break the condition, so every element must be read.

questions.text:
Consider a table \(T\), where the elements \(T[i][j]\), \(0 \leq i, j \leq n\), represent the cost of the optimal solutions of different subproblems of a problem that is being solved using a dynamic programming algorithm. The recursive formulation to compute the table entries is as follows:

\[T[0][k] = T[k][0] = 1 \quad \text{for } k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n\]
\[T[i][j] = 2T[i-1][j] + 3T[i][j-1] \quad \text{for } 1 \leq i, j \leq n\]

Consider the following two algorithms to compute entries of \(T\). Assume that for both the algorithms, for all \(0 \leq i, j \leq n\), \(T[i][j]\) has been initialized to 1.

```text
Algorithm B1:  For i = 1, 2, ..., n
                   For j = 1, 2, ..., n
                       T[i][j] = 2T[i-1][j] + 3T[i][j-1]

Algorithm B2:  For s = 2, 3, ..., 2n
                   For i = 1, 2, ..., n
                       For j = 1, 2, ..., n
                           If (i + j == s)
                               T[i][j] = 2T[i-1][j] + 3T[i][j-1]
```

Algorithm \(B_k\), \(k \in \{1, 2\}\) is said to be correct if and only if it calculates the correct values of \(T[i][j]\), for all \(0 \leq i, j \leq n\), (as per the recursive formulation) at the end of the execution of the algorithm \(B_k\).

Which one of the following statements is true?

options.label: B
options.text: Algorithm \(B_1\) is correct, but algorithm \(B_2\) is incorrect

options.label: C
options.text: Algorithm \(B_2\) is correct, but algorithm \(B_1\) is incorrect

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.solution:
Row 0 and column 0 are already 1 from the initialisation, as required. An entry \(T[i][j]\) needs \(T[i-1][j]\) and \(T[i][j-1]\) to be final before it is computed.

\(B_1\) fills row by row, left to right. When \(T[i][j]\) is computed, row \(i-1\) is complete and \(T[i][j-1]\) was computed just before. Correct.

\(B_2\) fills anti-diagonals \(i + j = s\) in increasing order of \(s\), each cell exactly once (every \(1 \leq i, j \leq n\) has \(2 \leq i + j \leq 2n\)). Both dependencies lie on diagonal \(s - 1\) (or on the border), which is finished earlier. Correct.

So both algorithms are correct.

questions.text:
Consider the following 4-variable Boolean function

\[F(A, B, C, D) = \Sigma m(0, 1, 2, 3, 8, 9, 10, 11)\]

Consider \(A\) as MSB, \(D\) as LSB. Which one of the following options represents the minimal sum of products form for the above function?

Note: + is OR operation, . is AND operation, ′ is NOT operation
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution: Minterms 0 to 3 are 00xx and minterms 8 to 11 are 10xx in \(ABCD\). Together they are exactly the eight minterms with \(B = 0\), whatever \(A\), \(C\), \(D\) are. So \(F = B'\).

questions.text:
Consider the canonical \(LR(0)\) parsing of the grammar below using terminals \(\{a, b, c\}\) and non-terminals \(\{A, B, C, S\}\) with \(S\) as the start symbol.

\[S \rightarrow ACB\]
\[A \rightarrow aA \mid \epsilon\]
\[C \rightarrow cC \mid \epsilon\]
\[B \rightarrow bB \mid b\]

Which one of the following options gives the number of shift-reduce conflicts that will occur in the \(LR(0)\) ACTION table?
questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.solution:
Build the LR(0) item sets for the augmented grammar \(S' \rightarrow S\). In LR(0) a complete item reduces on every terminal, so a state with a complete item and a shift on some terminal has a shift-reduce conflict.

\(I_0\): \(S' \rightarrow .S\), \(S \rightarrow .ACB\), \(A \rightarrow .aA\), \(A \rightarrow .\). Shift on \(a\) and reduce \(A \rightarrow \epsilon\): conflict 1.

On \(a\): \(A \rightarrow a.A\), \(A \rightarrow .aA\), \(A \rightarrow .\). Shift on \(a\) and reduce: conflict 2.

On \(A\) from \(I_0\): \(S \rightarrow A.CB\), \(C \rightarrow .cC\), \(C \rightarrow .\). Shift on \(c\) and reduce \(C \rightarrow \epsilon\): conflict 3.

On \(c\): \(C \rightarrow c.C\), \(C \rightarrow .cC\), \(C \rightarrow .\). Conflict 4.

On \(C\): \(S \rightarrow AC.B\), \(B \rightarrow .bB\), \(B \rightarrow .b\). No complete item, no conflict.

On \(b\): \(B \rightarrow b.B\), \(B \rightarrow b.\), \(B \rightarrow .bB\), \(B \rightarrow .b\). Shift on \(b\) and reduce \(B \rightarrow b\): conflict 5.

The remaining states (\(A \rightarrow aA.\), \(C \rightarrow cC.\), \(B \rightarrow bB.\), \(S \rightarrow ACB.\), \(S' \rightarrow S.\)) have only a single complete item. Each conflicting state has exactly one shift terminal, so there are 5 shift-reduce conflicts.

questions.text:
In the context of schema normalization in relational DBMS, consider a set F of functional dependencies. The set of all functional dependencies implied by F is called the closure of F. To compute the closure of F, Armstrong’s Axioms can be applied. Consider \(X\), \(Y\), and \(Z\) as sets of attributes over a relational schema. The three rules of Armstrong’s Axioms are described as follows.

Reflexivity: If \(Y \subseteq X\), then \(X \rightarrow Y\)

Augmentation: If \(X \rightarrow Y\), then \(XZ \rightarrow YZ\) for any Z

Transitivity: If \(X \rightarrow Y\) and \(Y \rightarrow Z\), then \(X \rightarrow Z\)

The additional rule of Union is defined as follows.

Union: If \(X \rightarrow Y\) and \(X \rightarrow Z\), then \(X \rightarrow YZ\)

It can be proved that the additional rule of Union is also implied by the three rules of Armstrong’s Axioms. Listed below are four combinations of these three rules. Which one of these combinations is both necessary and sufficient for the proof ?
questions.subject: Databases
questions.solution:
Proof of Union:

1. Augment \(X \rightarrow Y\) with \(X\): \(XX \rightarrow XY\), that is \(X \rightarrow XY\).

2. Augment \(X \rightarrow Z\) with \(Y\): \(XY \rightarrow YZ\).

3. Transitivity on steps 1 and 2: \(X \rightarrow YZ\).

Only Augmentation and Transitivity are used, so they are sufficient. Neither can be dropped: Transitivity alone cannot create a dependency whose right side is larger than any given right side, and Reflexivity with Augmentation alone cannot chain two dependencies. So Augmentation and Transitivity is the necessary and sufficient combination.

questions.text: Consider the transmission of data bits 110001011 over a link that uses Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) code for error detection. If the generator bit pattern is given to be 1001, which one of the following options shows the remainder bit pattern appended to the data bits before transmission?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.solution:
The generator 1001 has degree 3, so append three 0s: 110001011000. Divide by 1001 using XOR (modulo 2):

1100 XOR 1001 = 0101. Bring down bits: 1010 XOR 1001 = 0011. Next: 0111 (leading 0, no subtraction), then 1110 XOR 1001 = 0111, then 1111 XOR 1001 = 0110, then 1101 XOR 1001 = 0100, then 1000 XOR 1001 = 0001, then 0010, then 0100.

The remainder is 100, which is appended to the data.

questions.text: Consider a processor that has 16 general purpose registers and it uses 2-byte instruction format for all its instructions. Variable-sized opcodes are permitted. There are three different types of instructions; M-type, R-type, and C-type. Each M-type instruction has 2 register operands and a 6-bit immediate operand. Each R-type instruction has 3 register operands. Each C-type instruction has a register operand and a 6-bit offset value. If there are 2 unique M-type opcodes and 7 unique R-type opcodes, which one of the following options gives the maximum number of unique opcodes possible for C-type instructions?
questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.solution:
Instruction = 16 bits, register field = 4 bits.

M-type: \(4 + 4 + 6 = 14\) operand bits, so a 2-bit opcode: \(2^2 = 4\) patterns, 2 used, 2 left.

R-type: \(3 \times 4 = 12\) operand bits, so a 4-bit opcode. The 2 free 2-bit patterns give \(2 \times 2^2 = 8\) 4-bit patterns, 7 used, 1 left.

C-type: \(4 + 6 = 10\) operand bits, so a 6-bit opcode. The 1 free 4-bit pattern gives \(2^2 = 4\) 6-bit opcodes.

Maximum C-type opcodes = 4.

questions.text:
Consider the control flow graph given below.

Which one of the following options is the set of live variables at the exit point of each basic block?
questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.chapter: Code Optimisation and Data Flow Analysis
questions.solution:
Blocks: B1: a = b + c, with successors B2 and B3. B2: d = a + e, successor B4. B3: e = a + f, successor B1. B4: g = d + e, successor EXIT.

Use \(\text{IN}[B] = \text{use}[B] \cup (\text{OUT}[B] - \text{def}[B])\) and \(\text{OUT}[B]\) = union of IN of the successors, with nothing live at EXIT.

B4: OUT = \(\emptyset\), IN = \(\{d, e\}\).

B2: OUT = \(\{d, e\}\), IN = \(\{a, e\}\).

Start with IN[B1] = \(\{b, c\}\). B3: OUT = \(\{b, c\}\), IN = \(\{a, b, c, f\}\). B1: OUT = \(\{a, e\} \cup \{a, b, c, f\} = \{a, b, c, e, f\}\), IN = \(\{b, c, e, f\}\).

Again: B3: OUT = \(\{b, c, e, f\}\), IN = \(\{a, b, c, f\}\) (e is redefined). B1 does not change, so this is the fixed point.

OUT sets: B1 \(\{a, b, c, e, f\}\), B2 \(\{d, e\}\), B3 \(\{b, c, e, f\}\), B4 \(\emptyset\).

questions.text:
An index in a DBMS is said to be dense if an index entry appears for every search-key value in the indexed file. Otherwise it is called a sparse index. Consider the following two statements.

S1: A hash index must be a dense index

S2: A \(B^+\) tree index can be a sparse index

Which one of the following options is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Both S1 and S2 are true

options.label: B
options.text: Both S1 and S2 are false

options.label: C
options.text: S1 is true and S2 is false

options.label: D
options.text: S1 is false and S2 is true

questions.subject: Databases
questions.solution:
S1: a sparse index works only because the file is sorted on the search key, so a key missing from the index can be found by scanning forward from the nearest smaller entry. A hash index scatters keys over buckets with no order, so a key with no entry of its own cannot be located: every search-key value needs an entry. True.

S2: a \(B^+\) tree on a file sorted by its key (a clustering index) can keep one entry per data block, which is a sparse index. True.

questions.text:
Consider the following two finite automata \(D_1\) and \(D_2\).

Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.label: D
options.text: \((L(D_1) \cup L(D_2))^*\) consists of all strings in \(\{0,1\}^*\) whose length is divisible by 3

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.solution:
In both automata the start state is the only accepting state, and every path that leaves it returns after exactly 3 symbols.

\(D_1\): the cycles are 0 0 0, 0 0 1, 0 1 0 and 1 0 1. So \(L(D_1) = \{000, 001, 010, 101\}^*\).

\(D_2\): the cycles are 0 1 1, 1 1 1, 1 0 0 and 1 1 0. So \(L(D_2) = \{011, 111, 100, 110\}^*\).

A string in either language splits uniquely into 3-symbol blocks.

A: false, for example 000 is in \(L(D_1)\) but not in \(L(D_2)\).

B: false for the same reason.

C: a non-empty common string would need its first block in both block sets, but the two sets share no block. So the intersection is \(\{\epsilon\}\). True.

D: the two block sets together are all 8 strings of length 3, so \((L(D_1) \cup L(D_2))^* = (\{0,1\}^3)^*\), the strings whose length is divisible by 3. True.

questions.text:
Let \(\Sigma = \{a, b, c, d\}\) and let \(L = \{a^i b^j c^k d^\ell \mid i, j, k, \ell \geq 0\}\).

Which of the following constraints ensure(s) that the language \(L\) is context-free?
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.solution:
A: the condition is \(i - j + k - \ell = 0\), a single counter that goes up on \(a\) and \(c\) and down on \(b\) and \(d\). A PDA keeps it on the stack (with one symbol for a positive count and another for a negative count) and accepts if it ends at zero. Context-free.

B: \(a^i b^j c^i d^j\) needs two crossing comparisons (\(a\) with \(c\), \(b\) with \(d\)); by the pumping lemma it is not context-free.

C: \(a^i b^j c^j d^i\) is nested: \(S \rightarrow aSd \mid T\), \(T \rightarrow bTc \mid \epsilon\). Context-free.

D: push for every \(a\) and \(b\), pop for every \(c\) and \(d\), accept on an empty stack. Context-free.

questions.text:
Consider a binary search tree (BST) with \(n\) leaf nodes (\(n > 0\)). Given any node \(V\), the key present in the node is denoted as \(Val(V)\). All the keys present in the given BST are distinct. The keys belong to the set of real numbers.

For a node \(V\), let \(Suc(V)\) denote the node that is its inorder successor. If a node \(V\) does not have an inorder successor, then \(Suc(V)\) is \(NULL\). As there are no duplicates, if \(Suc(V)\) is not \(NULL\), then \(Val(V) < Val(Suc(V))\).

Corresponding to every leaf node \(L_i\) that has a non-NULL \(Suc(L_i)\), a new key \(k_i\) with the following property is to be inserted into the BST.

\[Val(L_i) < k_i < Val(Suc(L_i))\]

Let \(K\) represent the list of all such new keys to be inserted into the BST.

Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.label: B
options.text: \(K\) will have at least one element

options.label: C
options.text: After inserting all keys from \(K\), the height of the BST can increase at most by one

options.label: D
options.text: Number of nodes in the BST will double after inserting all keys from \(K\)

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.chapter: Trees, Binary Search Trees and Heaps
questions.solution:
Each \(k_i\) lies strictly between a leaf and the next key in sorted order. Different leaves give different consecutive pairs, so these open intervals are disjoint.

A: disjoint intervals give distinct keys. True.

B: false. If the BST is a single node, or a right-going chain, the only leaf is the largest key, it has no successor, and \(K\) is empty.

C: when \(k_i\) is inserted, the search follows the path to \(L_i\) (no existing key lies between \(L_i\) and \(k_i\)) and \(k_i\) becomes the right child of \(L_i\). Later insertions also land under their own leaves, since the intervals are disjoint. Every new node is a child of an old leaf, so the height grows by at most one. True.

D: at most \(n\) new nodes are added, while the tree also has internal nodes (for example a root with two leaves has 3 nodes and gets at most 1 new key, giving 4, not 6). False.

questions.text:
Consider a stack \(S\) and a queue \(Q\). Both of them are initially empty and have the capacity to store ten elements each. The elements 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 arrive one by one, in that order. When an element arrives, it is assigned either to \(S\) (pushed on \(S\)) or to \(Q\) (enqueued to \(Q\)). Once all the five elements are stored, the output is generated in two steps. First, stack S is emptied by popping all elements. Then queue \(Q\) is emptied by dequeueing all elements. The output obtained by following this process is 4 3 1 2 5 .

Given the output, the objective is to predict whether an element was assigned to \(S\) or \(Q\).

Which of the following options is/are possible valid assignment(s) of the elements?

Note: In the options, the notation \(xS\) denotes that element \(x\) was assigned to \(S\) and \(yQ\) denotes that element \(y\) was assigned to \(Q\).
questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.chapter: Arrays, Stacks, Queues and Linked Lists
questions.solution:
Elements arrive in increasing order, so the stack pops its elements in decreasing order and the queue releases its elements in increasing order. The output is the stack part (decreasing) followed by the queue part (increasing).

A: S = {1, 3, 4} pops 4 3 1, Q = {2, 5} gives 2 5. Output 4 3 1 2 5. Valid.

B: S = {3, 4} pops 4 3, Q = {1, 2, 5} gives 1 2 5. Output 4 3 1 2 5. Valid.

C: S = {4, 5} pops 5 4 first. Output starts with 5. Invalid.

D: S = {1, 2, 3} pops 3 2 1 first. Invalid.

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
The part from Wait(A) to Signal(A) is a critical section, so the three \(\texttt{*}\) are printed one process at a time. The process that makes X = 2 prints \(\texttt{\$}\) inside that same critical section, right after its \(\texttt{*}\). So every outcome starts \(\texttt{**\$}\) and has exactly one \(\texttt{*}\) after the \(\texttt{\$}\).

No \(\texttt{\#}\) can appear before \(\texttt{\$}\), because B starts at 0 and only the \(\texttt{\$}\) process signals it. After that, each process passing Wait(B) prints \(\texttt{\#}\) and signals B again, so all three \(\texttt{\#}\) are eventually printed.

A (\(\texttt{**\$*\#\#\#}\)): the third process enters its critical section before anyone prints \(\texttt{\#}\). Possible.

B (\(\texttt{**\$\#*\#\#}\)): one of the first two processes passes Wait(B) and prints \(\texttt{\#}\) before the third process prints \(\texttt{*}\). Possible.

C (\(\texttt{**\$\#\#*\#}\)): both of the first two processes print \(\texttt{\#}\) before the third process enters. Possible.

D (\(\texttt{***\$\#\#\#}\)): \(\texttt{\$}\) is printed by the second process to enter, before the third \(\texttt{*}\). Impossible.

questions.text:
Consider a system with a processor and a 4 KB direct mapped cache with block size of 16 bytes. The system has a 16 MB physical memory. Four words P, Q, R, and S are accessed by the processor in the same order 10 times. That is, there are a total of 40 memory references in the sequence P, Q, R, S, P, Q, R, S,…

Assume that the cache memory is initially empty. The physical addresses of the words are given below (1 word = 1 byte).

P: 0x845B32, Q: 0x845B26, R: 0x845B36, S: 0x846B32

Which of the following statements is/are true?

Note: \(1\text{K} = 2^{10}\) and \(1\text{M} = 2^{20}\)

options.label: A
options.text: Every access to P results in a cache miss

options.label: B
options.text: Every access to R results in a cache hit

options.label: C
options.text: Every access to Q results in a cache miss

options.label: D
options.text: Except the first access to S, all subsequent accesses to S result in cache hits

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.solution:
16 MB gives 24-bit addresses. Block size 16 B gives a 4-bit offset. Lines \(= 4\text{K} / 16 = 256\), an 8-bit index. Tag = 12 bits. So in a 6-hex-digit address, the first 3 digits are the tag, the next 2 the index, the last 1 the offset.

P: tag 845, line B3. Q: tag 845, line B2. R: tag 845, line B3 (same block as P). S: tag 846, line B3.

Round 1: P miss (loads 845 into B3), Q miss (B2), R hit, S miss (846 replaces 845 in B3).

Every later round: P miss (B3 holds 846), Q hit, R hit (P just reloaded the block), S miss.

A: true. B: true, R always follows P to the same block. C: false, Q hits after its first access. D: false, S always misses.

questions.text:
To keep track of free blocks in a file system, one of the two approaches is generally used – using bitmaps (bit vectors) or using linked lists. Consider that the linked list approach is used to keep track of free blocks in a file system. Assume that the disk size is 16 GB, block size is 2 KB, and block numbers used are 32-bit long. A single pointer of size 4 bytes is used in each block of the list to point to the next block of the list. The number of blocks required to hold the free disk block numbers is ____________. (answer in integer)

Note: \(1\text{K} = 2^{10}\) and \(1\text{G} = 2^{30}\)
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
Number of disk blocks \(= \frac{16 \text{ GB}}{2 \text{ KB}} = \frac{2^{34}}{2^{11}} = 2^{23} = 8388608\). Taking all of them as free, all these block numbers must be stored.

Each list block holds \(\frac{2048}{4} = 512\) four-byte entries, one of which is the pointer to the next list block, leaving 511 block numbers.

\[\left\lceil \frac{8388608}{511} \right\rceil = \lceil 16416.06 \rceil = 16417\]

questions.text:
A system has a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) that has a reach of 1 MB. TLB reach is defined as the total amount of physical memory that can be accessed through the TLB entries. The paging system uses pages of size 4 KB. The virtual address space is 64 GB and physical address space is 1 GB. If each TLB entry stores a 4-bit process id, page number, frame number, and a 2-bit control field, then the size of the TLB (in bytes) is ___________. (answer in integer)

Note: \(1\text{K} = 2^{10}\), \(1\text{M} = 2^{20}\), \(1\text{G} = 2^{30}\)
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
Entries \(= \frac{\text{reach}}{\text{page size}} = \frac{2^{20}}{2^{12}} = 256\).

Page number: \(64 \text{ GB} = 2^{36}\), so \(36 - 12 = 24\) bits. Frame number: \(1 \text{ GB} = 2^{30}\), so \(30 - 12 = 18\) bits.

Entry size \(= 4 + 24 + 18 + 2 = 48\) bits = 6 bytes.

TLB size \(= 256 \times 6 = 1536\) bytes.

questions.text:
Consider contiguous allocation of physical memory to processes using variable partitioning scheme. Suppose there are 8 holes in the memory of sizes 20 KB, 4 KB, 25 KB, 18 KB, 7 KB, 9 KB, 15 KB, and 12 KB. Assume that no two holes are adjacent. Two processes P1 of size 16 KB and P2 of size 9 KB arrive in that order, and they are allocated memory using the best-fit technique. After allocating space to P1 and P2, the number of holes of size less than 8 KB is ____________. (answer in integer)

Note: \(1\text{K} = 2^{10}\)
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution:
P1 (16 KB): the smallest hole of at least 16 KB is 18 KB, leaving a 2 KB hole.

P2 (9 KB): the 9 KB hole fits exactly, leaving no hole.

Holes now: 20, 4, 25, 2, 7, 15, 12 KB. Those below 8 KB: 4, 2, 7, so 3 holes.

questions.text:
Consider a system with 1 MB physical memory and a word length of 1 byte. The system uses a direct mapped cache, with block numbers starting from 0. The word with physical address 0xA2C28 is mapped to the cache block number \(176_{10}\). The maximum possible size of the cache (in KB) for this configuration is ___________. (answer in integer)

Note: \(1\text{K} = 2^{10}\) and \(1\text{M} = 2^{20}\)
questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.solution:
1 MB gives a 20-bit address: 0xA2C28 = 1010 0010 1100 0010 1000 (bits 19 down to 0).

With block size \(2^b\) and \(2^c\) cache lines, the line number is address bits \(b\) to \(b + c - 1\), and the cache size is \(2^{b+c}\). We need these bits to read \(176 = 10110000_2\), which needs \(c \geq 8\).

The pattern 10110000 occurs in the address only at bits 13 down to 6 (bits 13 to 6 are 1 0 1 1 0 0 0 0). So \(b = 6\). The index may extend upward while the extra bits are 0: bits 14, 15, 16 are 0 and bit 17 is 1. So the index can be bits 6 to 16, \(c = 11\).

Maximum cache size \(= 2^{6 + 11} = 2^{17}\) bytes \(= 128\) KB.

questions.text:
A non-pipelined instruction execution unit that operates at 1.6 GHz clock takes an average of 5 clock cycles to complete the execution of an instruction. To improve the performance, the system was pipelined with a goal of achieving an average throughput of one instruction per clock cycle. However, it could operate only at 1.2 GHz due to pipeline overheads. While executing a program in the pipelined design, 30% of instructions encountered a stall of 2 cycles due to pipeline hazards. The speed-up obtained by the pipelined design over the non-pipelined one for this program is ___________. (rounded off to two decimal places)

Note: \(1\text{G} = 10^9\)
questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.solution:
Non-pipelined time per instruction \(= \frac{5}{1.6 \text{ GHz}} = 3.125\) ns.

Pipelined CPI \(= 1 + 0.3 \times 2 = 1.6\), so time per instruction \(= \frac{1.6}{1.2 \text{ GHz}} = 1.3333\) ns.

\[\text{Speed-up} = \frac{3.125}{1.3333} = 2.34375 \approx 2.34\]

questions.text:
Consider a new TCP connection between a sender and a receiver. The receiver advertised window is constant at 48 KB, the maximum segment size (MSS) is 2 KB, and the slow start threshold for TCP congestion control is 16 KB. Assume that there are no timeouts or duplicate acknowledgements. The number of rounds of transmission required for the congestion control algorithm of the TCP connection to reach the congestion avoidance phase is ___________. (answer in integer)

Note: \(1\text{K} = 2^{10}\)
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.solution:
Slow start begins with cwnd = 1 MSS = 2 KB and doubles every round, while cwnd is below ssthresh = 16 KB. The receiver window (48 KB) never limits these windows.

Round 1: cwnd = 2 KB. Round 2: cwnd = 4 KB. Round 3: cwnd = 8 KB. Round 4: cwnd = 16 KB.

In round 4 the window has reached ssthresh, and TCP uses congestion avoidance once cwnd is at least ssthresh. So the connection is in congestion avoidance from the 4th round of transmission: the answer is 4.

questions.text:
Consider the digital circuit shown below with two input lines A and B, two select lines S0 and S1, and an output line Y. The blocks Q and M represent active high 2:4 decoder and 4-to-1 multiplexer, respectively. Out of 16 possible input combinations, the number of combinations that produce Y=1 is ____________. (answer in integer)

Note: One input combination is an instance of [A B S1 S0].
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution:
The decoder makes exactly one of D0 to D3 equal to 1. D0 = 1 only for A = 0, B = 0, and D3 = 1 only for A = 1, B = 1.

Multiplexer inputs: 0 from D0, 1 is constant 0, 2 is constant 1, 3 from D3.

S1 S0 = 00: Y = D0, 1 of the 4 (A, B) values.

S1 S0 = 01: Y = 0, none.

S1 S0 = 10: Y = 1, all 4.

S1 S0 = 11: Y = D3, 1.

Total \(= 1 + 0 + 4 + 1 = 6\).

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
Start: a = 5, b = 11, c = 20.

ptr = &a; *ptr = c sets a = 20.

ptr = &c.

a = *(&b) sets a = 11.

c = *ptr-a, where *ptr is c itself, gives \(c = 20 - 11 = 9\).

The program prints 9.

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution:
Only the length \(L = end + 1 - start\) matters. Each call changes it:

\(L \equiv 0 \pmod 3\): recurse with \(L - 1 \equiv 2\), adding nothing.

\(L \equiv 1 \pmod 3\): add 1 and recurse with \(L - 1 \equiv 0\).

\(L \equiv 2 \pmod 3\): recurse with \(L - 2 \equiv 0\), adding nothing.

From remainder 0 the length goes to remainder 2, and from 2 back to 0, so remainder 1 never occurs again. The 1 is added at most once (only when the first call has \(L \equiv 1\)), and the recursion ends at length below 1 returning 0.

For example func(0, 0) has \(L = 1\) and returns \(1 + \text{func}(0, -1) = 1\). The maximum possible value is 1.

questions.text: The determinant of a \(4 \times 4\) matrix A is 3. The value of the determinant of 2A is ____________. (answer in integer)
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
Multiplying an \(n \times n\) matrix by \(k\) multiplies each of its \(n\) rows by \(k\), so \(\det(kA) = k^n \det(A)\).

\[\det(2A) = 2^4 \times 3 = 48\]

questions.text:
Suppose an unbiased coin is tossed 6 times. Each coin toss is independent of all previous coin tosses. Let \(E_1\) be the event that among the second, fourth, and sixth coin tosses, there are at least two heads. Let \(E_2\) be the event that among the first, second, third, and fifth coin tosses, there are equal number of heads and tails.

The conditional probability \(P(E_1 \mid E_2)\) is equal to ____________. (rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
The two events share only toss 2.

Given \(E_2\) (2 heads among tosses 1, 2, 3, 5: \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) equally likely patterns), toss 2 is a head in 3 of them, so \(P(\text{toss 2} = H \mid E_2) = \frac{1}{2}\). Tosses 4 and 6 are independent of \(E_2\).

If toss 2 is H, \(E_1\) needs at least one head in tosses 4, 6: probability \(\frac{3}{4}\).

If toss 2 is T, \(E_1\) needs both tosses 4, 6 heads: probability \(\frac{1}{4}\).

\[P(E_1 \mid E_2) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{3}{4} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5\]

questions.text:
Consider a function \(f: (0,1) \rightarrow \{0, 1\}\) defined as follows.

For a real number \(r \in (0,1)\), \(f(r) = 1\) if the second digit after the decimal point in \(r\) is one of the four digits 2, 3, 6 and 7. Otherwise, \(f(r)\) is equal to 0.

The number of points in (0,1) at which \(f\) is discontinuous is ___________. (answer in integer)
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
The second digit is constant on each interval \(\left[\frac{k}{100}, \frac{k+1}{100}\right)\), where it equals \(k \bmod 10\). So \(f\) is constant inside each such interval and can only jump at \(r = \frac{k}{100}\), \(k = 1, \ldots, 99\), where the digit changes from \((k-1) \bmod 10\) to \(k \bmod 10\).

Values by digit: 0, 1 give 0; 2, 3 give 1; 4, 5 give 0; 6, 7 give 1; 8, 9 give 0. The value changes at the steps 1 to 2, 3 to 4, 5 to 6 and 7 to 8, and not at 9 to 0. So there is a jump when \(k \bmod 10 \in \{2, 4, 6, 8\}\).

Each of the 10 tens (\(k = 0\) to 9, 10 to 19, ..., 90 to 99) gives 4 such \(k\): \(10 \times 4 = 40\) points of discontinuity.

questions.text:
It is necessary to design a link-layer protocol between two hosts that are directly connected over a lossless link of length 3000 kilometers. Assume that the link bandwidth is \(10^8\) bits per second and that the propagation delay in the link is 5 nanoseconds per meter. Every transmitted data byte is assigned a unique sequence number.

Let \(N\) be the minimum number of bits needed for the sequence number field in the protocol header such that

i. the sequence numbers do not wrap around before 60 seconds, and

ii. the maximum utilization of the link is achieved.

The value of \(N\) is ______. (answer in integer)
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.solution:
Condition i: in 60 s the link carries \(\frac{10^8 \times 60}{8} = 7.5 \times 10^8\) bytes, each with its own number. \(2^{29} \approx 5.37 \times 10^8\) is too small and \(2^{30} \approx 1.07 \times 10^9\) is enough, so at least 30 bits.

Condition ii: propagation delay \(= 3 \times 10^6 \text{ m} \times 5 \text{ ns/m} = 15\) ms, so RTT = 30 ms. Full utilization needs a window of \(10^8 \times 0.03 = 3 \times 10^6\) bits \(= 3.75 \times 10^5\) bytes, which needs only about 19 to 20 bits (even doubled for a sliding window). 30 bits already covers it.

\(N = 30\).
